\chapter{More of the Body}
\label{ch:ka-more-body}
\hlchaptermodality{57}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five more parts of a person in Kannada, and say where it hurts.}

\section[kuttige]{\kn{ಕುತ್ತಿಗೆ} (kuttige) — the neck}

\label{lesson:KA-C57-neck}



\begin{quote}
Before the new run: what did \emph{pātre} mean, and what did \emph{peṭṭige} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಕುತ್ತಿಗೆ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಕುತ್ತಿಗೆ}} (\emph{kuttige}) — \textquotedblleft{}the neck\textquotedblright{}.

The everyday word, and the one a \kn{ವೈದ್ಯ} uses. Kannada has a second, \kn{ಕೊರಳು} (\emph{koraḷu}), and the two divide by what is being done to the neck rather than by which part of it is meant: \kn{ಕೊರಳು} is the neck a \kn{ಹೂಮಾಲೆ} goes around and the neck a voice comes out of, while \kn{ಕುತ್ತಿಗೆ} is the neck that aches.

So a singer's is a \kn{ಕೊರಳು} and a patient's is a \kn{ಕುತ್ತಿಗೆ}, and the same piece of a person is both, depending on why you brought it up.

This chapter picks up where the leg and the tooth left off, and the run gets less obvious as it goes.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five more pieces of a person.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{kuttige}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{nanna kuttige} — \textquotedblleft{}my neck\textquotedblright{} — with the possessing word in front
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಕುತ್ತಿಗೆ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the neck\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bennu]{\kn{ಬೆನ್ನು} (bennu) — the back}

\label{lesson:KA-C57-back}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{kuttige} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಬೆನ್ನು}}
\textbf{\kn{ಬೆನ್ನು}} (\emph{bennu}) — \textquotedblleft{}the back\textquotedblright{}.

Inherited, and it opens with the \emph{b} that has now turned up in \kn{ಬಾಗಿಲು}, \kn{ಬೇರು} and \kn{ಬೆಟ್ಟ}. Four words in four chapters, and by this point you should be reading that first letter as a small piece of history rather than as a sound.

\kn{ಬೆನ್ನು} is the part of a person that faces away, so the language uses it for anything behind you. \kn{ಬೆನ್ನ} \kn{ಹಿಂದೆ}, behind the back, is where things are said about you that would not be said in front.

And \kn{ಬೆನ್ನು} \kn{ತಟ್ಟು}, to pat the back, means to praise or encourage — the same gesture English named the same way, with no contact between the two languages at any point. Some pictures are simply what bodies do.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two, and this one has a hand on it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bennu}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{bennu}, then \emph{bēru}, then \emph{beṭṭa}, and hear the one letter they share
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಬೆನ್ನು} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the back\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tuṭi]{\kn{ತುಟಿ} (tuṭi) — a lip}

\label{lesson:KA-C57-lip}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{bennu} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ತುಟಿ}}
\textbf{\kn{ತುಟಿ}} (\emph{tuṭi}) — \textquotedblleft{}a lip\textquotedblright{}.

Two syllables, inherited, and here the four sisters go four different ways. Tamil, Malayalam and Telugu each reach for something quite unlike \kn{ತುಟಿ} and unlike each other. For a family this close that is unusual, and it usually means the part in question got renamed after the family split, several times over, by whichever picture each language happened to prefer.

\kn{ತುಟಿ} sits directly on the \kn{ಬಾಯಿ} you already have. The mouth is the opening; the \kn{ತುಟಿ} is its edge.

And it is the piece of the face that Kannada uses for keeping quiet. To say nothing at all is to not move the \kn{ತುಟಿ} — a phrase built out of a body part rather than out of a word for silence, which is how a great many everyday expressions in this language are put together.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three, and this one edges a word you already had.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tuṭi}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{bāyi}, then \emph{tuṭi}, and say which one is the edge of the other
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ತುಟಿ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a lip\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bhuja]{\kn{ಭುಜ} (bhuja) — the shoulder}

\label{lesson:KA-C57-shoulder}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{tuṭi} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಭುಜ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಭುಜ}} (\emph{bhuja}) — \textquotedblleft{}the shoulder\textquotedblright{}.

Sanskrit \emph{bhuja}, and behind it \emph{bhuj-}, \textquotedblleft{}to bend\textquotedblright{}. The shoulder is named for being the joint that folds — the limb described by what it does rather than by where it sits. Sanskrit built a good many body words that way.

Kannada's own word here is \kn{ಹೆಗಲು} (\emph{hegalu}), and the division between the two is worth having. \kn{ಹೆಗಲು} is the shoulder you carry a load on, the flat top of it; \kn{ಭುಜ} leans toward the joint and toward strength — the arm-and-shoulder of somebody who can lift things.

That opening \kn{ಭ} is a letter Kannada mostly uses in borrowed words. Meeting one is a fair hint that the word came from Sanskrit before you know anything else about it.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four, and this is the run's borrowed one.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{bhuja}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{bhuja}, then \emph{kuttige}, and say which of the two the \kn{ಹೂಮಾಲೆ} passes
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಭುಜ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the shoulder\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[mūḷe]{\kn{ಮೂಳೆ} (mūḷe) — a bone}

\label{lesson:KA-C57-bone}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what did \emph{bhuja} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \kn{ಮೂಳೆ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಮೂಳೆ}} (\emph{mūḷe}) — \textquotedblleft{}a bone\textquotedblright{}.

Here Kannada is the odd one out. Tamil says \emph{elumbu}, Malayalam says \emph{eluvu}, Telugu says \emph{emuka} — three sisters plainly holding the same old word between them, and Kannada holding \kn{ಮೂಳೆ}, which is not it.

That happens. A language drops an inherited word and promotes another one, and afterwards the family tree looks broken at exactly one branch. The ear-word and the nose-word each showed you a version of this earlier, with a different sister standing apart each time. Which one is the odd one out changes from word to word, and that is the whole point: these are four separate languages, not four accents.

\kn{ಮೂಳೆ} closes the body run, and it is the piece of you that outlasts the rest.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \kn{ಕುತ್ತಿಗೆ}, \kn{ಬೆನ್ನು}, \kn{ತುಟಿ}, \kn{ಭುಜ}, \kn{ಮೂಳೆ}. Enough to say where it hurts.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{mūḷe}
  \item it once more, slowly
  \item all five in order, then say which of them is the odd one in the family
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \kn{ಮೂಳೆ} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a bone\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
